section_summary: This section documents Japanese censorship of American books, magazines, and newspapers between 1936 and 1939, including exclusions for alleged lèse-majesté, indecency, criticism of the Japanese Army, and threats to public order. It also covers American efforts to have prohibited books returned rather than confiscated and a police ban on reporting military measures in Japan’s southwestern territories and northern Korea. The final documents concern suppression of Yukio Ozaki’s argument that Japan should remain neutral in a future European war.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 162 on the Suppression of Current History’s May Issue
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the stated reason for suppression in Japan of the May issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: Current History’s selling agent personally asked the Censor’s Office why the May issue had been suppressed. The office attributed the action to Charles Hodges’s article “Japanese Enigma.”

subfiles.title: Letter to Current History Explaining the Suppression of Its May Issue
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Relays the American Embassy’s information concerning the suppression of Current History in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State informs Current History that its selling agent in Japan consulted the Censor’s Office. According to the agent, the May issue was suppressed because it contained Charles Hodges’s “Japanese Enigma.”

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment from Current History
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Department’s correspondence concerning suppression of the magazine’s May issue.
subfiles.summary: Current History thanks the Department of State for its letters of July 29 and 30. Those letters supplied additional information about the suppression of its May issue in Japan.

subfiles.title: Disposition of American Books Excluded from Japan
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports an effort to secure the return, rather than confiscation, of American books denied entry into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dickover forwards a letter from W. S. Hall of Snyder & Hall, which handled export business for numerous American publishers. Hall sought permission for rejected books to be returned to their American senders because the prevailing practice was apparently confiscation. The Embassy also gave the Japanese Foreign Office an informal memorandum, and the chief of its Bureau of American Affairs promised an investigation.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. S. Hall on Confiscation of Imported Books
subfiles.about: Protests the confiscation of foreign books and asks that prohibited titles instead be returned to their senders.
subfiles.summary: Hall accepts Japan’s authority to ban books but objects to their destruction or confiscation, which imposes losses on Japanese booksellers and discourages orders from American publishers. He argues that returning prohibited books would protect Japan equally well without injuring legitimate trade. He stresses that the firms he represents do not sell erotic or pornographic works and that no Japanese bookseller asked him to make the appeal.

subfiles.title: Informal Memorandum on Returning Excluded American Books
subfiles.to: Chief, Bureau of American Affairs, Japanese Foreign Office
subfiles.about: Requests a change in Japanese practice so that excluded American books may be returned instead of confiscated.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that uncertainty about which books will be prohibited discourages Japanese buyers from placing normal orders for new American titles. It contends that returning excluded books would still protect Japan while avoiding unnecessary losses to the American book industry.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Ban of Fortune
subfiles.about: Records an understanding of why Fortune magazine was banned.
subfiles.summary: The note states that Fortune was banned because it discussed matters falling under press censorship. It provides no further detail about the issue or the particular passages involved.

subfiles.title: American Books and Magazines Recently Excluded from Japan
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Lists foreign books and periodicals recently denied entry into Japan and their reported grounds for exclusion.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reports the exclusion of the September 1936 issues of Fortune and The Literary Digest for alleged lèse-majesté, all issues of Film Fun for indecency, and Victor Yakhontov’s Eyes on Japan for passages concerning the “Cult of the Mikado.” He observes increased Japanese activity against foreign publications. As an exception, Henry L. Stimson’s The Far Eastern Crisis was admitted after apparent opposition to a ban from the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Press Ban on Certain Military Measures
subfiles.about: Reports police instructions restricting publication of information about military measures in several Japanese-controlled regions.
subfiles.summary: On February 4, Japanese newspapers were instructed to publish nothing except official War and Navy Ministry statements about military measures in Japan’s southwestern islands, Taiwan, the Ogasawara Islands, or northern Korea. Grew notes that such bans had previously been used either to conceal operations in progress or to prevent unfounded rumors. The Embassy did not know which explanation applied in this instance.

subfiles.title: Internal Note on Confiscation of American Periodicals
subfiles.about: Summarizes the reported reasons for confiscating American periodicals in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note records that the Embassy in Tokyo had reported confiscation of certain American periodicals. It attributes the actions to several causes, especially perceived disrespect toward the Emperor and criticism of the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: American Magazines Recently Excluded
subfiles.about: Reports the confiscation of the March Living Age and April Esquire in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Citing the Tokyo Asahi of May 6, Grew reports that the March issue of Living Age was confiscated because of a remark deemed disrespectful to the Emperor. The April issue of Esquire was confiscated over a caricature of a Japanese general as a “Lawrence of Japan” and accompanying criticism of the Japanese Army’s policy toward China.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy of “American Magazines Recently Excluded”
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on Japanese confiscation of Living Age and Esquire.
subfiles.summary: This degraded duplicate repeats the report that Living Age was confiscated for disrespect toward the Emperor. It also repeats that Esquire was suppressed because of a caricature comparing a Japanese general to Lawrence and criticism of Japanese Army policy in China.

subfiles.title: Internal Note on Suppression of the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs; Ballantine
subfiles.about: Summarizes the suppression of the July 4 Japan Advertiser over an article by Yukio Ozaki advocating neutrality.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the Japan Advertiser was suppressed for publishing Ozaki’s argument that Japan should remain neutral in the next world war. It suggests that censors may have objected to his contention that Germany and Italy could offer Japan no compensation for entering the war on their side. Ozaki predicted that neutrality could leave Japan able to control the Far East and perhaps the world.

subfiles.title: Suppression of Japan Advertiser of July 4, 1939
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports and explains police suppression of a Japan Advertiser issue containing Yukio Ozaki’s neutrality article.
subfiles.summary: Dooman transmits Ozaki’s article and judges that its frank discussion of Japan’s relations with Germany and Italy probably caused the suppression under a public-order provision of the press law. Ozaki argued that neutrality in another European war would generate prosperity, help meet the costs of the conflict in China, and leave Japan and the United States as the principal surviving powers. Copies already distributed were not recalled, but remaining copies at the newspaper’s office were confiscated. Nippon Hyoron, which originally published the article, and Contemporary Opinions, which translated it, were suppressed in the same limited manner.

subfiles.title: Riches, Power Seen for Japan if Neutral in Next World War
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping; enclosure to despatch No. 4014
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan should remain neutral in a future European war to avoid destruction and gain wealth and international power.
subfiles.summary: Ozaki maintains that Japan’s near-neutrality during the First World War produced extraordinary growth in national wealth and that another European conflict could similarly offset the costs of the China campaign. He rejects alignment with Germany and Italy because they have little to offer and warns that fighting the Anglo-French-American powers would exact a ruinous price. He also invokes Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita’s limited interpretation of the Anti-Comintern Pact and argues that it should not draw Japan into an unrelated war. Neutrality, he concludes, could leave Japan and the United States as the two strongest surviving powers, whereas participation would bring ruin regardless of victory or defeat.
